{"id": "295752b2-a40b-4d8b-8057-21e0559f891d", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_vAZCKNvYQvOLFMt4mph8C0", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Scaling and throughput best practices\",\"context\":\"## `bedrock-mantle` endpoint: throughput and quotas\\n\\nThe `bedrock-mantle` endpoint has the following quota behavior:\\n\\n* Models with published quotas have separate per-model, per-Region input-tokens-per-minute and output-tokens-per-minute quotas.\\n* The endpoint does not enforce RPM quotas. Two workloads with the same RPM can consume very different amounts of capacity, so plan and rate-limit by tokens and concurrency instead of RPM alone.\\n* When a request is admitted, the input-token check includes the input tokens plus the requested `max_tokens` value. After the response completes, the unused part of that reservation is replenished. Set `max_tokens` no higher than your application needs.\\n* Models without published TPM quotas do not currently have per-account TPM quotas exposed in Service Quotas. This does not mean that throughput is unlimited; internal service capacity and transient rate limiting still apply.\\n* Batch inference and Provisioned Throughput are available only through `bedrock-runtime`. Service-tier and model support varies by model.\\n\\nDefault values and your account's allocations can vary by model, Region, and usage history. For current values, quota evaluation details, and the AWS Support process for requesting an increase, see Quotas for the bedrock-mantle endpoint. See the applicable Models at a glance for model-specific endpoint, service-tier, and feature support\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/scaling-throughput-best-practices.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Quotas for the bedrock-mantle endpoint\",\"context\":\"## How requests are evaluated against quotas\\n\\nWhen you submit an inference request to the `bedrock-mantle` endpoint, AWS evaluates it against your quotas in the following order:\\n\\n1. **Input tokens per minute** \u2013 The number of input tokens in the request, plus the value of `max_tokens` (or the model-specific maximum if `max_tokens` is not set), is checked against the input-tokens-per-minute quota for the requested model. If admitting the request would exceed the quota, the request is throttled with an HTTP 429 response.\\n2. **Output tokens per minute** \u2013 As the model streams or generates output, output tokens are counted against the output-tokens-per-minute quota for that model. If the quota is reached during generation, generation stops and the response is returned with a finish reason indicating the cutoff.\\n\\nAfter the response completes, any unused portion of the initial input-token reservation (the difference between `max_tokens` and the actual output) is replenished to your quota.\\n\\nThe endpoint may apply additional internal rate limiting that is not exposed in Service Quotas. Use retry logic with exponential backoff to handle transient throttling.\\n\\nThe `bedrock-runtime` endpoint's TPM quotas count input and output tokens together against a single per-model quota, while the `bedrock-mantle` endpoint applies separate input-tokens-per-minute and output-tokens-per-minute quotas. If you run workloads on both endpoints, plan capacity for each endpoint independently. For details on the runtime endpoint's quotas, see Quotas for the bedrock-runtime endpoint\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-mantle.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Global cross-Region inference for latest Anthropic Claude Opus, Sonnet and Haiku models on Amazon Bedrock in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Taiwan | Artificial Intelligence\",\"context\":\"### Understanding quotas and planning for scale\\n\\nAmazon Bedrock enforces service quotas to support fair resource allocation and system stability. For Global CRIS, quotas are measured in two dimensions, each serving a distinct purpose in capacity management:\\n\\n* **Tokens per minute (TPM)** \u2013 The maximum number of tokens (input + output) that can be processed per minute.\\n* **Requests per minute (RPM)** \u2013 The maximum number of inference requests that can be made per minute.\\n\\nDefault quotas vary by model and are allocated per source Region. You can view your current quotas in the AWS Service Quotas console by navigating to Amazon Bedrock service quotas in your source Region (Singapore or Jakarta).\\n\\nAmazon Bedrock uses a token burndown rate that weighs output tokens more heavily than input tokens when calculating quota consumption. The burndown rate is 5:1, meaning output tokens consume five times more quota than input tokens because generating tokens requires more computation than processing input.\\n\\n`Quota consumption = Input tokens + (Output tokens \u00d7 5)`\\n\\nFor example, if your request uses 10,000 input tokens and generates 5,000 output tokens:\\n\\n`Total quota consumption = 10,000 + (5,000 \u00d7 5) = 35,000 tokens`\\n\\nThe request consumes 35,000 tokens against your TPM quota for throttling purposes. When planning capacity requirements and requesting quota increases, you need to account for this burndown rate in your calculations. If your application processes requests with this same token pattern at 100 requests per minute, the total quota consumption would be 3,500,000 TPM (100 requests \u00d7 35,000 tokens per request). When working with your AWS Account Manager on quota increase requests, provide your expected request volume, average input tokens per request, and average output tokens per request so they can calculate the appropriate quota allocation using this burndown multiplier\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/global-cross-region-inference-for-latest-anthropic-claude-opus-sonnet-and-haiku-models-on-amazon-bedrock-in-thailand-malaysia-singapore-indonesia-and-taiwan/\"},{\"rank_order\":4,\"title\":\"Accelerate generative AI innovation in Canada with Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference | Artificial Intelligence\",\"context\":\"## Quota management for Canadian workloads\\n\\nWhen using CRIS from Canada, quota management is performed at the source Region level (`ca-central-1`). This means quota increases requested for the Canada (Central) Region apply to all inference requests originating from Canada, regardless of where they\u2019re processed.\\n\\n### Understanding quota calculations\\n\\n**Important:** When calculating your required quota increases, you need to take into account the burndown rate, defined as the rate at which input and output tokens are converted into token quota usage for the throttling system. The following models have a 5x burn down rate for output tokens (1 output token consumes 5 tokens from your quotas):\\n\\n* Anthropic Claude Opus 4\\n* Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.5\\n* Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4\\n* Anthropic Claude 3.7 Sonnet\\n\\nFor other models, the burndown rate is 1:1 (1 output token consumes 1 token from your quota). For input tokens, the token to quota ratio is 1:1. The calculation for the total number of tokens per request is as follows:\\n\\n`Input token count + Cache write input tokens + (Output token count x Burndown rate)`\\n\\n### Requesting quota increases\\n\\nTo request quota increases for CRIS in Canada:\\n\\n1. Navigate to the AWS Service Quotas console in the Canada (Central) Region\\n2. Search for the specific model quota (for example, \u201cClaude Sonnet 4.5 tokens per minute\u201d)\\n3. Submit an increase request based on your projected usage\\n\\n### Migrating from older Claude models to Claude 4.5\\n\\nOrganizations currently using older Claude models should plan their migration to Claude 4.5 to leverage the latest model capabilities.\\n\\nTo plan your migration strategy, incorporate the following elements:\\n\\n1. **Benchmark current performance**: Establish baseline metrics for your existing models.\\n2. **Test with representative workloads and optimize prompts**: Validate Claude 4.5 performance with your specific use cases, and adjust prompt to leverage Claude 4.5\u2019s enhanced capabilities and make use of the Bedrock prompt optimizer tool.\\n3. **Implement gradual rollout**: Transition traffic progressively.\\n4. **Monitor and adjust**: Track performance metrics and adjust quotas as needed\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/accelerate-generative-ai-innovation-in-canada-with-amazon-bedrock-cross-region-inference/\"},{\"rank_order\":5,\"title\":\"How do I troubleshoot the \\\"ThrottlingException\\\" error when I use Amazon Bedrock on-demand resources?\",\"context\":\"### Monitor your AWS service quotas\\n\\nReview your [Amazon Bedrock service quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas.html) to make sure that you didn't exceed them. Check Amazon CloudWatch metrics at 1-minute increments to identify throttling patterns. When your usage exceeds the quotas at peak times, resource throttle can occur even with previously successful batches. To make sure that your application's request volume doesn't exceed the quotas, monitor the\u00a0**InputTokenCount** and **Invocations** [Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/monitoring-runtime-metrics.html).\\n\\nSpecific models have separate quotas for Requests Per Minute (RPM) and Tokens Per Minute (TPM) that Amazon Bedrock enforces concurrently.\\n\\nNewer model versions can have different quotas than previous versions.\\n\\n**Note:** The Service Quota dashboard shows only configured quotas, not real-time usage. To monitor real-time usage, use CloudWatch\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/bedrock-throttling-error\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Search AWS docs for Bedrock mantle endpoint quotas and billing names"}

See the applicable Models at a glance for model-specific endpoint, service-tier, and feature support\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/scaling-throughput-best-practices.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Get started with OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra, and Luna on Amazon Bedrock | Artificial Intelligence\",\"context\":\"## Quotas and scaling\\\\n\\\\nWhen you invoke GPT-5.6 models, requests use on-demand inference on the Standard service tier, where you pay per token without reserving capacity.\\\\n\\\\nInference on the bedrock-mantle endpoint is governed by two per-model, per-Region quotas, one for input tokens per minute and one for output tokens per minute. There is no requests-per-minute quota. Cached input tokens read through prompt caching do not count against the input-tokens-per-minute quota, which is one more reason caching helps at scale. If a token-per-minute quota is exceeded, the endpoint returns an HTTP 429 response. Handle transient throttling with exponential backoff and a bounded retry count, which the OpenAI SDK supports through its `max_retries` setting. For more information, refer to Quotas for the bedrock-mantle endpoint.\\\\n\\\\nOne recommended way to handle transient throttling is exponential backoff with a bounded retry count. The OpenAI SDK supports this through its `max_retries` setting:\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nfrom aws_bedrock_token_generator import provide_token\\\\nfrom openai import BedrockOpenAI\\\\n\\\\nregion = \\\\\"us-east-1\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\nclient = BedrockOpenAI(\\\\n aws_region=region,\\\\n bedrock_token_provider=lambda: provide_token(region=region),\\\\n max_retries=6,\\\\n)\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nTo reduce throttling on sustained high volume, spread large workloads across multiple minutes rather than firing them in tight bursts, and increase request rates gradually so throughput can track regional capacity\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/get-started-with-openai-gpt-5-6-sol-terra-and-luna-on-amazon-bedrock/\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Quotas for the bedrock-mantle endpoint\",\"context\":\"## View quota values\\\\n\\\\nQuota values vary by model, account, and AWS Region. Each quota name identifies the model and\\\\nwhether the value applies to input or output tokens per minute\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-mantle.html\"},{\"rank_order\":4,\"title\":\"Quotas for Amazon Bedrock\",\"context\":\"# Quotas for Amazon Bedrock\\\\n\\\\nYour AWS account has default quotas, formerly referred to as limits, for Amazon Bedrock. To view\\\\nservice quotas for Amazon Bedrock, do one of the following:\\\\n\\\\n* Follow the steps at Viewing service\\\\n quotas and select **Amazon Bedrock** as the service.\\\\n* Refer to the Amazon Bedrock service quotas in the AWS General Reference.\\\\n\\\\nModel inference in Amazon Bedrock is controlled by quotas on token usage. Some models use tokens at a higher rate. Use the RPM quota when you plan capacity or request a quota increase for an embedding model. For more information, see Amazon Titan Text Embeddings models.\\\\n\\\\nAmazon Bedrock offers two inference endpoints \u2013 `bedrock-runtime` and `bedrock-mantle` \u2013 each with its own per-model quota allocations. For details, see Quotas for the bedrock-runtime endpoint and Quotas for the bedrock-mantle endpoint.\\\\n\\\\nTo maintain the performance of the service and to ensure appropriate usage of Amazon Bedrock, the\\\\ndefault quotas assigned to an account might be updated depending on regional factors,\\\\naccount age, usage history, payment history, fraudulent usage, and/or approval of a quota increase request.\\\\nAs a result, the quotas that apply to your account might be lower than the default values\\\\nlisted in the Amazon Bedrock service quotas. When using the OpenAI SDK, you need an Amazon Bedrock API key. For production workloads, use short-term API keys. They expire automatically (maximum 12 hours) and inherit the permissions of the IAM role that generated them. If you are already using native AWS credentials and don\u2019t have an API key, the aws-bedrock-token-generator package generates a short-term bearer token from those credentials.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nfrom openai import OpenAI\\\\n\\\\nclient = OpenAI(\\\\n api_key=\\\\\"<your-short-term-bedrock-api-key>\\\\\",\\\\n base_url=\\\\\"https://bedrock-mantle.us-east-1.api.aws/openai/v1\\\\\",\\\\n)\\\\n\\\\nresponse = client.chat.completions.create(\\\\n model=\\\\\"google.gemma-4-31b\\\\\",\\\\n messages=[\\\\n {\\\\\"role\\\\\": \\\\\"user\\\\\", \\\\\"content\\\\\": \\\\\"Explain the benefits of mixture-of-experts architectures for production inference.\\\\\"}\\\\n ],\\\\n max_tokens=512,\\\\n)\\\\nprint(response.choices[0].message.content)\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nIf you are migrating an existing application that already uses the OpenAI SDK format with a different model, the migration typically requires updating only the base URL and the model ID. When these conflict with the documentation results above or with what you remember, prefer the most recent dated source.\\n\\n{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Amazon Bedrock expands support for Service Quotas - AWS\",\"context\":\"Amazon Bedrock, a managed service for enterprise-grade access to high-performing foundation models from leading AI companies, now supports viewing inference quotas for the bedrock-mantle endpoint through AWS Service Quotas. {"id": "5f0c8500-ef51-46dc-9e3e-383274b9030c", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "The "mantle" in the line name strongly suggests your traffic goes through `bedrock-mantle`. I couldn't find documentation that says so, and your own client code is the better check.

**What the docs confirm**
- Bedrock has two inference endpoints, `bedrock-runtime` and `bedrock-mantle`. Each has its own per-model quotas, and traffic is tracked separately even for the same model.
- `bedrock-mantle` quotas are per model and per Region, split into input tokens per minute and output tokens per minute. There is no RPM quota.
- If you do run on mantle, the input check is input tokens plus the requested `max_tokens`. Any unused part is returned after the response completes. A high `max_tokens` can therefore cause 429s even when your actual input is small.
- On `bedrock-runtime`, input and output tokens count together against one per-model TPM quota. Those are different quotas from the mantle ones.

**What I couldn't confirm**
- I found nothing that documents how Cost Explorer usage types are named, or that "mantle" in a usage type maps to the endpoint. Mantle is the inference engine behind the `bedrock-mantle` endpoint, so the inference is reasonable. It's still an inference.

**How to be sure**
- Check the base URL or SDK your application uses. A `bedrock-mantle.<region>.api.aws` URL means mantle. The OpenAI SDK, the Anthropic Messages API and `BedrockOpenAI` all point to it. The Bedrock `Converse` or `InvokeModel` APIs mean `bedrock-runtime`.
- Check whether you see the same model under a non-mantle usage type. If you do, you may be using both endpoints, and each needs its own capacity plan.
- In Service Quotas, open Amazon Bedrock and search for "bedrock-mantle endpoint". Look for the Claude Sonnet 5 input and output tokens-per-minute entries in `us-east-1`. The `USE1` prefix in your line items points to that Region.
